clue.text: Imbecile somehow ran Amazon?

indicators.note: an imbecile scheme is a senseless one, so the letters that follow lose their sensible order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An insult aimed at some fool who ran the online retailer Amazon, badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imbecile' looks like the noun the clue is about, but it is an adjective working as the anagram signal; Amazon is the warrior woman, not the company.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amazons of Greek legend were mounted female warriors, so a strong rider of the other sex fits the name.

clue.text: Taking top off, had a fling in partnership

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the opening letter, and taking it off removes that letter

parts.note: to dally is to flirt or have a light affair

explanation.surface: Someone stripping off after a brief affair with a business partner.
explanation.walkthrough: DALLIED loses its first letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: Allied describes parties joined by agreement or alliance, working together as a pair or group.

clue.text: Peanuts regularly in novel, large Swiss roll's filling

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Emma is the Jane Austen novel

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A bizarre recipe with peanuts in the filling of a big Swiss roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swiss roll' is not the cake: read it as a bread roll from Switzerland, and its filling is a Swiss cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmental is the holey Swiss cheese, exactly what might be stuffed into a sandwich roll in Switzerland.

clue.text: Bishop saw elevated character who's a bit of an ass

definitions.text: character who's a bit of an ass

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters up the column makes them read upwards, last letter first

parts.note: a saw is a saying or maxim

explanation.surface: A churchman viewing some lofty person who behaves like a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Saw is the noun meaning an old saying, not the verb or the tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick Bottom the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream is given a donkey's head, and a bottom is also literally part of one's backside.

clue.text: My bad food, consuming case of Cointreau and pop

indicators.note: to consume is to take inside oneself, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: a meal is food eaten at one sitting

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outermost letters are wanted

parts.note: first and last letters
pop and pa are both words for father

explanation.surface: Apologising for a poor dinner that came with orange liqueur and fizzy drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop suggests fizzy drink but means dad here.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are admissions of fault: the Latin phrase meaning through my fault and the modern slang apology.

clue.text: Slight, short sound from sucker

indicators.note: something short is cut off before its end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: the noise made sucking a drink through a straw

explanation.surface: A faint, brief noise made by something that sucks.
explanation.walkthrough: Slight looks like an adjective meaning small, but it is a noun meaning an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: A slight and a slur are both remarks or acts that disparage someone's reputation.

clue.text: Don, say, headgear before Scottish smoker

parts.note: a hood covers the head
lum is Scots for a chimney, which smokes

explanation.surface: Putting on a hat before lighting up a pipe in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Don looks like the verb to put on clothes, which fits headgear, but it is a Mafia boss.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mafia don is an example of a gangster or violent criminal, which is what the answer denotes.

clue.text: Teacher has slop on bread — the chop's coming!

parts.note: the head teacher of a school
swill is liquid slops fed to pigs
a bread roll

explanation.surface: A school cook serving dreadful food to a teacher who is about to be sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts the earlier pieces above the bread.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom predicts people will be dismissed or punished, just as getting the chop means being fired.

clue.text: Lie on front, hiding face and thighs

indicators.note: a face is the leading side, and concealing it removes the opening letter

parts.note: a front is a cover or disguise
the lap is the top of the thighs when seated

explanation.surface: Lying face-down, hiding one's face and legs.
explanation.walkthrough: Front seems to go with lying down, but it is a cover story; COVER drops its C.
explanation.definitionFit: When one thing lies partly on top of another the two are said to overlap.

clue.text: It removes coat or undies worn by one traveller

indicators.note: a garment worn by someone surrounds them, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: pants are underpants in British English
the Roman numeral for one
a tripper is someone on a day trip

explanation.surface: Something that takes off one's coat or underwear, worn by a lone traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: Coat suggests a garment, as do the undies, but it is a coat of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Paint-stripper is a solvent that lifts layers of old paint off wood or metal.

clue.text: Dry wine bottles cool after six-pack?

parts.note: a six-pack is a set of well-defined abdominal muscles, or abs

indicators.note: to bottle something is to shut it inside, so one piece closes around another

parts.note: tent is a deep red Spanish wine
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A dry wine chilled after a six-pack of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Six-pack looks like beer cans, but it is a toned stomach; dry is teetotal, not a wine description.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry person avoids alcohol entirely, which is what abstinent means when applied to drinking.

clue.text: Men plugging means to animate old palace companion

indicators.note: a plug fills a hole, so one piece is stuffed inside another

parts.note: computer-generated imagery, used in animation
other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Soldiers promoting a way to bring back to life an old friend at the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: The late Queen Elizabeth II famously kept corgis at Buckingham Palace.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Elizabeth II kept these short-legged Welsh dogs as pets throughout her reign, hence the royal link.

clue.text: As some say, blade did some cutting

indicators.note: what some people say is spoken, so the word is judged by its pronunciation in certain accents

parts.note: a sword is a blade; in non-rhotic accents it matches the past tense of a cutting verb

explanation.surface: A knife's edge carried out some trimming, as people claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As some say' hedges the sound match: only in accents that drop the R does the weapon sound like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To saw is to cut with a toothed blade, so the past tense means did some cutting.

clue.text: Stir a lot of citrus fruit, and appeal for date to finish

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter goes

parts.note: stir is slang for prison, where one does time
a green citrus fruit
it means sex appeal

explanation.surface: Stir plenty of orange into a recipe, and ask for a date for completion.
explanation.walkthrough: Stir is prison slang, not the kitchen verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadline is a date by which work must be finished, which is a limit in time.

clue.text: Yours truly, so fit, spinning the bottle

parts.note: the setter refers to themself
so and thus both mean therefore

indicators.note: to spin is to turn round, so the letters face the opposite way

parts.note: hale means healthy

explanation.surface: Someone boasting they are healthy while playing spin the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bottle' sounds like the party game, but it is a particular size of wine bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A methuselah is a large champagne or wine bottle holding eight standard bottles, about six litres.

clue.text: Wrong person setting exam that absorbs two minutes

indicators.note: to absorb is to take something in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the setter refers to themself
an oral is a spoken examination
M is the abbreviation for minute, twice

explanation.surface: An unsuitable examiner writes a test lasting just a couple of minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's I and the ORAL together swallow the two Ms between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrong in the ethical sense means contrary to accepted principles of right conduct.

clue.text: Order something on plate, people tucking into it

parts.note: the registration shown on a car's number plate

indicators.note: tucking into means pushing inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
men are people

explanation.surface: Ordering food on a plate that diners then start eating.
explanation.walkthrough: Plate suggests dinner, but it is a car's number plate; tucking into is eating in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To regiment is to organise strictly, imposing order and discipline on people or things.

clue.text: Two pints then eight emptied, or four

parts.note: a quart is two pints

indicators.note: emptying something takes out its contents, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A pub-crawl tally: a couple of pints, then eight drained, or maybe four.
explanation.walkthrough: Numbers here are units and words to trim, not counts of drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A quartet is a group or set of four, most often four musicians playing together.

clue.text: Continue expedition, eating starter from Italian grill

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: a quest is a journey in search of something
on as in carry on

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Carrying on a trip after grabbing something from an Italian grill restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: Grill looks like a restaurant noun, but it is the verb meaning to interrogate.
explanation.definitionFit: To grill someone is to interrogate them intensely, putting a series of searching queries to them.

clue.text: Old noble German? Get serious!

parts.note: to land something is to get it
grave means solemn or serious

explanation.surface: Mocking an aristocrat from Germany with a scornful exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get serious!' reads as an exclamation of disbelief, but is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A landgrave was a count with territorial jurisdiction in the Holy Roman Empire, a historic German title.

clue.text: It makes clothing market that shuts in November

indicators.note: shutting something in encloses it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: an agora was a Greek marketplace
N is November in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A clothes-making business at a market which closes for the month of November.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shuts in November' reads as seasonal closure, but it encloses the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Angora is soft wool from rabbits or goats, spun and knitted into jumpers and other garments.

clue.text: Catherine II's son is an eminent scientist

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Russian tsar who succeeded Catherine the Great, with his regnal numeral
second meaning: the Austrian Nobel-winning physicist of the exclusion principle

explanation.walkthrough: The regnal numeral matters: Tsar PAUL I, written with Roman I, spells the surname of the physicist Wolfgang PAULI.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolfgang Pauli formulated the exclusion principle in quantum mechanics and won the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics.

clue.text: Harry Potter, on vacation, touring east of France and Spain

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all round it, so one piece surrounds another
vacated means emptied, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: first and last letters
est is French for east
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: The boy wizard on holiday, travelling through eastern France and Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Potter reads as the wizard, but Harry is a verb meaning to harass.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry someone is to harass or badger them persistently, which is what pester means.

clue.text: Quietly leaving stage, getting censure

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so a letter drops out of the word

parts.note: a podium is a raised stage
p is piano, the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: A performer slips off the stage quietly after being criticised.
explanation.walkthrough: PODIUM loses its P.
explanation.definitionFit: Odium is general disapproval or opprobrium, the condemnation heaped on someone who is disliked.

clue.text: This person's a leader in Mecca?

definitions.text: This person's a leader in Mecca?

parts.note: the setter speaking: I am, shortened
taken as written

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A person announcing that they lead prayers in Mecca.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the speaker is a prayer leader.
explanation.definitionFit: An imam leads the congregational prayers in a mosque, so one might well lead worship in Mecca.

clue.text: Drop off returning ex-PM, drunk after drive

indicators.note: coming after something means following it, so the earlier words are placed second

parts.note: drive and go as in energy or push

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel, a former Prime Minister
a sot is a drunkard

explanation.surface: Dropping a former prime minister home, drunk after a car trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop off seems to mean giving someone a lift, and drunk looks like an adjective; both mislead.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop off is an idiom for falling asleep, usually without meaning to.

clue.text: Run into less chubby person training

indicators.note: going into something puts it inside, so one piece enters another

parts.note: less fat
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Bumping into a slimmer person at the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: Run into suggests meeting someone by chance.
explanation.definitionFit: A learner is someone being taught a skill, such as a trainee or a pupil driver.

clue.text: Exposed poet's entreaty to songwriter?

parts.note: O is the poetic cry of appeal
the plea to write a tune: pen a melody

explanation.surface: A revealed poem in which the poet begs a composer to write a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the whole wordplay as a poet crying 'O, pen air!' to a songwriter: pen means write, and an air is a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open-air is outdoors, uncovered and exposed to the elements.
